barriers.description: The study sample was small and not representative of the larger HSCT caregiver population, limiting the breadth of user data available to designers.
barriers.justification: Limited and non-representative sampling constrained designers' ability to manage user understanding and to specify user requirements that generalize across diverse caregiver contexts, reducing confidence in evaluation and iteration decisions.
barriers.reference_excerpt: First, although we collected data from three different transplant centers, our sample sizes are not representative of the larger HSCT caregiver population. Future work should include large, diverse samples of caregivers with varying levels of health literacy.

barriers.description: The study omitted HSCT recipients, so designers lacked the recipient perspective needed to understand dyadic interactions and dual needs.
barriers.justification: Not including recipients prevented designers from addressing the holistic caregiver–recipient experience and hindered their ability to fully understand context of use and to specify requirements that consider both parties.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Second, our study did not include HSCT recipients. A future direction of our work is to build knowledge of how HIT-enabled tools can dually benefit caregivers and HSCT recipients.

barriers.description: Transplant providers reported they have little insight into caregiver burden after discharge, limiting the observational and clinical data available to the design team.
barriers.justification: Providers' limited post-discharge contact constrained designers' ability to understand the real-world context of use and to manage evolving user understanding over the full care trajectory, impeding requirements specification and evaluation for post-discharge support.
barriers.reference_excerpt: All three transplant centers admit they have little insight about burden on caregivers after discharge, as much of the interaction with caregivers is pre- and during the HSCT.

barriers.description: There is a sparse evidence base of prior HIT interventions for HSCT caregivers, with nearly all existing interventions delivered in-person.
barriers.justification: A limited precedent of technology-enabled interventions reduced designers' available domain knowledge and examples to draw on when specifying user requirements, producing design solutions, and planning evaluations tailored to this population.
barriers.reference_excerpt: We found that few interventions for HSCT caregivers leverage HIT [10]. Our review indicated that nearly all caregiver interventions were delivered in-person. Only one study used a technology-enabled intervention.
